title: The New Old Middle East
gist: Gulf scholar F. Gregory Gause III argues the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran that began in February 2026 and the June 2026 cease-fire have left the region structurally unchanged: Iran's IRGC-dominated regime emerged stronger after demonstrating a chokehold over the Strait of Hormuz and striking Gulf energy facilities, Israel has settled into permanent-war disruption without diplomacy, and the Abraham Accords momentum has reversed. He argues the only durable fixes are a Hormuz management framework, a nuclear modus vivendi with Tehran, and Palestinian self-determination — none of which is being pursued.

themes.theme: Continuity Thesis: Sound and Fury, No New Order

insights.claim: Despite direct Iranian-Israeli homeland strikes, the fall of Assad and the flattening of Gaza, the Middle East emerging from the 2023-2026 upheaval structurally resembles the prewar region: outside powers play balance-of-power games inside weak Arab states, the Iranian-Israeli conflict endures, the Palestinian question is unresolved, and the United States can neither impose order nor leave.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: Argues against pricing any durable Middle East peace dividend into energy or regional risk premia — the same conflict drivers remain loaded.
insights.locator: All these changes are real and important

insights.claim: The U.S.-Israeli war launched in February 2026 to sap Iranian power instead gave the Islamic Republic a new lease on life, leaving the prewar regime largely intact and now dominated by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: An IRGC-dominated Tehran with proven escalation tools implies higher, not lower, baseline risk to Gulf energy infrastructure going forward.
insights.locator: The cease-fire signed by Iran and the United States in June 2026

insights.claim: Because none of the underlying dynamics or interests in the Middle East have changed, even a more sustainable cease-fire only starts the countdown to the next war.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: Treat cease-fire headlines as tactical, not structural — geopolitical risk discounts should not be fully removed on truce news.
insights.quote: the countdown to the next war will have already begun
insights.locator: And because there has been no meaningful change

insights.claim: A genuinely transformed Middle East would require stronger central governments in Iraq, Lebanon, Syria and Yemen capable of policing borders and preventing nonstate actors from running their own foreign policies, because weak states cannot make durable peace.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete checklist for judging whether any peace framework is real — state capacity, not signing ceremonies, is the test.
insights.quote: Weak states, after all, cannot make durable peace.
insights.locator: A truly changed Middle East, one that could be the basis

insights.claim: Neither Washington nor Tehran is willing to escalate in a way that changes the fundamentals, since Iran will not allow unfettered Hormuz shipping, surrender its nuclear program or abandon its proxies, while the United States will not send the ground troops that externally imposed regime change would require.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: Implies a persistent grinding conflict equilibrium rather than either resolution or all-out war — a chronic, recurring shipping and insurance risk.
insights.locator: At the time of this writing, Iran and the United States were alternating

insights.claim: Military force cannot produce a better regional order: the United States and Israel cannot bomb their way to a better region.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: The author's core policy verdict — kinetic escalation should be read as risk-additive with no compensating structural upside.
insights.quote: The United States and Israel cannot bomb their way to a better region.
insights.locator: The United States and Israel cannot bomb their way

insights.claim: Between October 2023 and February 2026 Iran looked like a paper tiger: its nuclear infrastructure was reduced to rubble by Israeli and U.S. strikes in June 2025, Israel killed generals and nuclear scientists on Iranian soil and assassinated Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh in Tehran, and Assad's December 2024 fall severed Iran's land bridge to Lebanon.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: Establishes the baseline of Iranian weakness that made the 2026 escalation look attractive — and against which its recovery should be measured.
insights.locator: Between October 7, 2023, and February 28, 2026

insights.claim: Iranian security forces killed at least 7,000 protesters during the December 2025 wave of economically driven protests according to the Human Rights Activists News Agency, with other organizations estimating the toll in the tens of thousands.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: Quantifies domestic instability that persists beneath Iran's external strength — sanctions-relief desperation is a real negotiating lever.
insights.locator: Persistent economic problems triggered a wave of protests

insights.claim: Iran regained regional prominence by defying the U.S.-Israeli onslaught and discovering its leverage over world energy markets, exercising a chokehold over the Strait of Hormuz and assaulting its Gulf neighbors' energy facilities, airports and hotels.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: Tehran has now demonstrated and internalized an energy-market weapon it previously only threatened — a structural upward shift in oil tail risk.
insights.locator: Yet Iran emerged victorious from this latest round

insights.claim: Having survived direct attack, Iran now has every incentive to develop nuclear weapons as the ultimate deterrent against future Israeli and American strikes.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: The war likely accelerated rather than halted weaponization — proliferation headlines and further strike cycles are the base case.
insights.locator: And it will have every incentive to do whatever it can

insights.claim: Iran's regional policy of the past 47 years — opposition to Israel, resistance to American power, and involvement in the politics of weak Arab states — will continue unchanged under the IRGC-dominated leadership that replaced the supreme leader of 36 years.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: Leadership change in Tehran should not be traded as policy change; proxy activity continues regardless of who holds the office.
insights.locator: It will certainly continue with the fundamental elements

themes.theme: Proxy Network: Down but Not Out

insights.claim: Iran-aligned Shiite parties and militias performed well in Iraq's November 2025 elections, then lobbed missiles at U.S. bases in February, March and April 2026, and the new Iraqi government under Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has filled important positions with Iran's local allies.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: Iraqi political capture by Iran-aligned actors keeps U.S. bases and Iraqi oil infrastructure inside the escalation perimeter.
insights.locator: In Iraq’s elections in November 2025

insights.claim: Israel's 2026 ground invasion and nationwide air campaign in Lebanon killed over 4,200 people and displaced one million, and its likely victim is not Hezbollah — which has survived more than 40 years of conflict — but the new Lebanese government that condemned Hezbollah's attack and offered to negotiate.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: Military campaigns against proxies discredit the reformist governments that could actually disarm them — a self-defeating loop that keeps Lebanon a failed-state risk.
insights.locator: But the task of restoring the state’s primacy in Lebanon

insights.claim: The Houthis stayed out of the first half of 2026 fighting because of a cease-fire with Saudi Arabia maintained since 2022, during which Riyadh paid the salaries of Yemeni civil servants working under Houthi control.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: Saudi payments were the actual mechanism keeping Red Sea shipping calm — its breakdown, not ideology, is the trigger to monitor.
insights.locator: The Houthis, Iran’s ally in Yemen, snarled global shipping

insights.claim: The Houthis have declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia, with uncertain but probably damaging effects on Red Sea energy flows, and are likely to rejoin the regional conflict on Iran's behalf.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: Red Sea and Bab el Mandeb disruption is re-arming as a live shipping-rate and tanker-routing risk alongside Hormuz.
insights.locator: At the time of this writing, the Houthis had declared a naval blockade

themes.theme: Gulf States: Entrapment, Abandonment, and No Alternative Patron

insights.claim: Gulf governments kept a low profile during the June 2025 strikes on Iran and lobbied Washington against attacking in early 2026 because war threatens the tourism, trade and foreign investment they need to diversify away from energy exports.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: Gulf diversification agendas (giga-projects, tourism, FDI) are directly hostage to escalation — a headwind for Vision-2030-style investment programs.
insights.locator: For years, the Gulf countries have favored stability

insights.claim: Gulf restraint failed to protect them: when the U.S.-Israeli war began in February 2026 it was the Gulf that bore the brunt of Iranian retaliation, illustrating the textbook weak-ally dilemma of simultaneous fear of entrapment and abandonment.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: A reusable model for allied behavior: expect hedging rhetoric but continued dependence, and expect Gulf assets to absorb retaliation risk.
insights.locator: This restraint didn’t help the Gulf countries with Iran

insights.claim: The June 2026 U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding alarmed the Gulf states because it neglected to mention them or address Iranian missile and drone capabilities, yet they all supported it fearing that further U.S. escalation would bring renewed strikes on their territory.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: Any U.S.-Iran deal that omits missiles and drones leaves Gulf energy infrastructure structurally exposed regardless of headline de-escalation.
insights.locator: The memorandum of understanding signed by Iran and the United States

insights.claim: The Gulf states cannot pivot away from Washington because American technology and training underpin the air defenses that successfully repelled Iranian drones and missiles, and no substitute guarantor exists — China lacks both the desire and the power projection, Russia sides with Iran and is consumed by Ukraine, and Europe, Egypt, Pakistan and Turkey cannot match U.S. fighting capability.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: Undercuts the 'Gulf drifts to Beijing' narrative — U.S. defense exports and basing arrangements retain a structural monopoly.
insights.locator: Yet despite their frustration, the Gulf countries are unlikely

insights.claim: Momentum for expanding the Abraham Accords has stalled and Gulf warming toward Israel has reversed, with the United Arab Emirates the only Gulf state to recommit, after Israel's September 2025 strike on a residence in Qatar and its war on Iran convinced Gulf leaders that Israel disregards their security.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: Saudi-Israeli normalization — long treated as an inevitable catalyst — should be discounted; the political cost to Arab leaders has risen sharply.
insights.locator: What has changed over the past three years is the Gulf’s view of Israel

insights.claim: Israel has decided to play regional disruptor on the confidence that military prowess alone can protect it indefinitely — a questionable bet given that its hard power was similarly impressive before October 7.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: The core risk case on Israel: deterrence-by-force without diplomacy has already failed once and leaves a permanent security-spending and mobilization burden.
insights.quote: Israel has decided to play regional disruptor, confident that its military prowess is enough to protect it indefinitely.
insights.locator: Even when Israel did come out on top in the wars

insights.claim: The June 2026 cease-fire left Iran in power with enough military assets to assert itself regionally and without any concrete obligation to give up its nuclear program, and Washington also conceded Tehran's demand that the cease-fire extend to Lebanon.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: Measures the war's actual yield against its stated aims — no verified nuclear rollback means the strike cycle can restart at any time.
insights.locator: The June 2026 U.S.-Iranian cease-fire left the Islamic Republic in power

insights.claim: Netanyahu's belief that Israel is safer when its neighbors are weak and divided ignores that Israel's most enduring security has come from peace treaties with Egypt and Jordan, consolidated states able to control their borders and suppress violent nonstate actors.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: A predictive rule: Israeli security correlates with neighboring state strength, so policies that weaken Beirut and Damascus raise long-run Israeli risk.
insights.locator: Netanyahu believes that Israel is safer when its neighbors are weak

insights.claim: Israel is actively obstructing state-building in Lebanon and Syria despite U.S. support for the new governments — capturing a Syrian buffer zone, arming Druze militias, encouraging Druze resistance to Damascus and striking Syrian army positions including the Ministry of Defense headquarters.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: U.S. and Israeli objectives in the Levant are openly divergent — Syrian reconstruction and reopening trades face continuing Israeli interference risk.
insights.locator: In Syria, Israel captured a so-called buffer zone

insights.claim: The only time Washington successfully disciplined Netanyahu was after Israel bombed Qatar in September 2025, when Trump forced a public apology to the emir and pressured him into accepting the Gaza cease-fire.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that U.S. leverage over Israeli conduct exists but is used only when a Gulf partner is directly hit — a narrow, predictable trigger.
insights.locator: Only when Israel’s hubris led it to bomb Qatar

themes.theme: Gaza and the West Bank: Cease-Fire as Respite

insights.claim: Israeli forces have killed over 1,000 Palestinians since the October 2025 cease-fire took effect, still occupy roughly 70 percent of Gaza, Hamas refuses to disarm despite its truce commitment, and the international security force in Trump's 20-point plan has never materialized.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: The Gaza cease-fire is a pause, not a settlement — Gaza reconstruction and investment plans rest on an unbuilt security foundation.
insights.quote: The Gaza cease-fire looks more like a respite in the conflict than an end to it.
insights.locator: Violence continues in Gaza itself

insights.claim: Netanyahu's government has ruled out any Palestinian Authority role in Gaza and had still not permitted the plan's committee of Palestinian technocrats to enter the territory as of July 2026, making post-Hamas governance nearly impossible.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: Without a credible Palestinian counterparty, third-country security forces and development capital will stay on the sidelines indefinitely.
insights.locator: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government has been crystal clear

insights.claim: During 2025 Israeli soldiers and settlers killed 240 Palestinians in the West Bank and Israel approved 54 new settlements, the highest annual total since the 1993 Oslo accords, followed by February 2026 legislation making it easier for settlers to buy West Bank land.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: De facto annexation is proceeding through settlement approvals and land law — a slow-burn trigger for the next escalation and for European sanctions pressure.
insights.locator: During 2025, Israeli soldiers and settlers killed 240 Palestinians

insights.claim: The October 7 attack demonstrated that as long as Palestinian self-determination remains unrealized, Palestinian refusal to accept the status quo can blow up the Middle East, yet no U.S. government has been willing to apply the leverage on Israel that a political solution would require.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: The Palestinian question is modeled as the region's recurring detonator — an unhedged tail risk for regional assets on any multi-year horizon.
insights.locator: An even more transformative U.S. policy would require grasping the nettle

themes.theme: Syria Under Shara: The One Real Change

insights.claim: The single most significant geopolitical change of the past three years is the fall of the Assad regime and the rise of Ahmed al-Shara, a former al-Qaeda member who has cultivated U.S., Turkish, EU and Arab support and pulled Syria out of the Iranian alliance maintained since the 1980s.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: The genuine structural shift to trade: Syria's realignment durably degrades Iran's Levant reach and opens sanctions-relief-driven reconstruction exposure.
insights.locator: By far the most significant geopolitical change

insights.claim: Syria's realignment has considerably reduced Iran's ability to shape Lebanese politics and threaten Israel from Syrian territory, a real blow to Tehran's regional influence.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: Hezbollah's resupply corridor is structurally impaired, which caps the scale though not the existence of future Lebanon escalation.
insights.locator: These changes have also considerably reduced Iran’s ability

insights.claim: Syria remains a weak state whose forces have clashed with Alawites in the west, Druze in the south and Kurds in the northeast, and if that weakness lures Iran, Israel, Turkey or the Gulf states into another round of civil war, prospects for regional stability could vanish.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: Syrian reconstruction exposure carries renewed-civil-war risk; sectarian clash frequency is the leading indicator to watch.
insights.locator: His reassuring words aside, Syria remains deeply divided

insights.claim: The Trump administration has backed Syria's new government by lifting sanctions, embracing President Shara, and in February 2026 handing the al-Tanf base to the Syrian military, ending a U.S. presence in Syria dating to 2014.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: Sanctions relief plus U.S. withdrawal is the practical opening for Gulf and Turkish capital into Syrian reconstruction.
insights.locator: He has lifted sanctions on Syria and embraced its new president

themes.theme: Policy Prescriptions: Hormuz Governance and a Nuclear Modus Vivendi

insights.claim: Regional stability requires the United States to sustain its Gulf military footprint — the Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain, Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, 5,000 to 10,000 troops in Kuwait, and base access in Oman and the UAE — because without it Iran can threaten its neighbors at will and Gulf states may yield to Iranian pressure on oil policy and relations with Israel.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: Explicitly links the U.S. basing posture to OPEC-relevant oil policy — a U.S. drawdown would be a bullish-risk signal for crude, not a peace signal.
insights.locator: Any progress toward regional stability will require the United States

insights.claim: Oman's foreign minister disclosed that just before the February 2026 offensive Iranian diplomats had floated a deal under which Iran would never stockpile enriched uranium, and despite Iran's stronger post-war position its desperation for sanctions relief makes that proposal a viable starting point for new negotiations.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: A concrete, previously-tabled deal contour to watch for — sanctions relief on Iranian crude is the tradable outcome if talks revive.
insights.locator: Oman’s foreign minister indicated that just before

insights.claim: The United States should lead a multilateral framework for managing the Strait of Hormuz with China, India, the United Kingdom and European, Gulf and Southeast Asian states, modeled on the Suez Canal and Turkish Straits conventions or the Strait of Malacca system in which a private foundation funds hydrographic surveys, navigational infrastructure and wreck removal from voluntary contributions.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: Recognizes Hormuz has become a governance problem, not just a military one — any such framework would be the single biggest structural de-risking event for oil.
insights.locator: Separately, the United States should lead a multilateral effort

insights.claim: Regime change through war in Iran has clearly failed as a strategy, leaving diplomacy toward a sustainable modus vivendi with Tehran as the only remaining route to calming the region.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: If Washington accepts this verdict, expect a pivot back to negotiations and eventual Iranian barrels; if not, expect repeat strike cycles.
insights.quote: The alternative strategy, regime change through war, has clearly failed.
insights.locator: Even though American leverage in these talks

insights.claim: The region's players are unchanged — an emboldened Iran with scores to settle, proxies that are down but not out, and an Israel that has come to accept near-permanent war instead of compromise — so the stage is set for the next conflagration.
insights.speaker: F. Gregory Gause III
insights.so_what: The closing forecast: assume recurring regional escalation as the base case for multi-year energy and shipping risk assumptions.
insights.quote: The stage is set for the next conflagration.
insights.locator: The region’s players have not changed
